titleStmt.title: The Knitting Leaflet Project: piloting crowdsourcing as a method of extracting quantifiable data from knitting pattern leaflets

dhq:bio.p: Dr Eleanor Reed is a Lecturer in English at Brunel, University of London. Her research focuses on class and gender in domestic women’s magazines within wider literature, 1900s–1950s; she is currently researching how these publications contributed to the development of knitting in Britain during this period. Her first monograph, Woman’s Weekly and Lower-Middle-Class Domestic Culture in Britain, 1918–1958: Making Homemakers was published by Liverpool University Press in 2023. She belongs to the editorial committee of the Journal of European Periodical Studies.

Dr Hugh Dickinson is a lecturer in astrophysics at the Open University. He has over 10 years experience working with the Zooniverse platform to design and manage citizen science projects. In that time, he has contributed as a research team member to 19 Zooniverse projects, providing expertise in project design, project management, data analysis and data interpretation.

dhq:abstract.p: The rise of digital and digitised archives is offering scholars of periodicals new methods of distant reading serialised texts that are too large to be read in full by a single researcher. The Knitting Leaflet Project piloted online crowdsourcing as a method of collecting quantitative data from a large corpus of knitting pattern leaflets. Hosted on free online crowdsourcing platform Zooniverse, it set out to explore three questions. Is it possible to crowdsource data from knitting pattern leaflets on Zooniverse? Can crowdsourced data, analysed quantitatively, reveal trends in knitting pattern leaflets over time? What lessons does this project offer to future research? Unfortunately, issues with the project’s design led to flaws in the quantitative data collected. As a result, the data were unusable, and the first and second questions could not properly be answered. Nevertheless, the project had three key successes. Firstly, it engaged precisely the community it aimed to reach – enthusiastic and expert knitters, who enjoyed participating. Secondly, while the quantitative data were flawed, some valuable qualitative data were collected, highlighting the potential of Zooniverse for hosting alternative forms of crowdsourcing. Finally, participant feedback enabled structural issues in the project to be identified, suggesting ways in which these could be avoided in future. Piloting a new method of data collection through community engagement, the project and its findings are of interest to researchers in the fields of fashion and textile history, periodical studies, Digital Humanities, and GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, Museums) sector organisations.

dhq:teaser.p: A pilot project, crowdsourcing quantitative and qualitative data from historic knitting pattern leaflets on citizen science platform Zooniverse. What worked, what didn't work, and why.

div.head: Preamble
div.p: The Knitting Leaflet Project (KLP) was a leap into the dark. Like many scholars of periodicals, I am intrigued by methods of distant reading bodies of text that are too large to be read by a single researcher. A social scientist suggested that online crowdsourcing platform Zooniverse could be used to collect data that, analysed quantitatively, might reveal trends in a periodical text over time. With my background in non-digital literary scholarship, I mostly conduct my research in archives, close-reading print copies of early to mid-twentieth-century women’s magazines, with specific focus (most recently) on their knitting features. Crowdsourcing and quantitative analysis were beyond my knowledge and experience. Nevertheless, I was intrigued. I knew from my public talks and workshops that many knitters are enormously knowledgeable about the handicraft and its history. Given the size of online knitting communities, a project to crowdsource data from knitting features in a periodical might work. Following my 2019–2020 postdoctoral research in the Collection of the Knitting & Crochet Guild (KCG), I had access to a potential dataset: scans of knitting pattern leaflets published between the 1900s and the 1980s. So, when the opportunity arose to attend a Zooniverse project-building workshop, I took it, and the KLP was the result. Co-author Hugh Dickinson assisted with the project-building and then downloaded the data and made it readable; but I (Eleanor Reed) did everything else (workflow and task design, project publicity, volunteer recruitment, data analysis, writing this article). The KLP was therefore a pilot, conceived and run by a curious non-expert, who wanted to find out if its methods could work with a view to re-running with funding and appropriate expertise if they did.

I share this background as context. Due to my lack of knowledge and experience, there were issues with the KLP’s design that led to flaws in the quantitative data collected. Nevertheless, it had three key successes. Firstly, it engaged precisely the community I wanted to reach – enthusiastic and expert knitters, including people who recalled knitting during the 1950s, who obviously enjoyed participating. Secondly, while the quantitative data were flawed, some highly valuable qualitative data were collected, highlighting the potential of Zooniverse for hosting alternative forms of crowdsourcing. Finally, participant feedback enabled me to identify structural issues that led to flaws in the data and suggest ways in which these might be avoided in future. I offer this article as a case study: a critical discussion with implications for research by others as well as myself.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The KLP piloted a novel, digital method of collecting and interpreting data from a large corpus of multimodal printed texts: crowdsourcing and quantitative analysis. A collection of images from 3000+ knitting pattern leaflets printed between around 1900 and 1980, owned by UK charity the KCG, was uploaded to Zooniverse, and data were extracted from it by a global community of citizen volunteers. Data extraction involved classification tasks, in which volunteers looked at images from the leaflets and responded to multiple-choice questions about their publication decade, contents, and appearance. Their responses were collected in a database, which was downloaded and analysed quantitatively to see if it could yield information about the leaflets’ development over the twentieth century. A pilot, it explored three questions. Is it possible to crowdsource data from knitting pattern leaflets on Zooniverse? Can crowdsourced data, analysed quantitatively, reveal trends in knitting pattern leaflets over time? What lessons does this project offer to future research? I consider these questions in the Results and Discussion section below. First however, I introduce knitting pattern leaflets as a distinctive print form within the constellation of twentieth-century women’s periodicals, situate the KLP within a growing intersection between periodical studies and the Digital Humanities, and outline the methods piloted. The project and its findings are of interest to researchers in the fields of fashion and textile history, periodical studies, and Digital Humanities, along with GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, Museums) sector organisations.

div.head: Context – knitting, pattern leaflets, reading ‘big’ texts, digital analysis
div.p: The twentieth century saw significant developments in knitting and knitwear in Britain. Between the 1900s and the 1930s, knitting in Britain exploded in popularity, and knitwear became high fashion. During the First and Second World Wars, knitting constituted national service, and knitters churned out clothing and other comforts for those serving in harsh conditions. Knitting also provided escapism, links to peacetime life, and a means of coping with shortages – it retained this last function throughout the post-Second World War period of austerity. As prosperity returned during the 1950s, knitting kept its association with thrift – but also provided new opportunities to spend, the quantity and variety of patterns and yarns having risen. Enthusiasm for knitting fell during the 1960s, with the increasing availability of factory-made knitwear, but rose again during the 1970s and 1980s, within a more general revival of crafting (see ; ; ; , , ; ). Knitting pattern leaflets drove these developments. Paper leaflets containing instructions for making one or a small number of knitted items, they were introduced around the 1900s by yarn manufacturers, to showcase their products among mass female audiences. Although the patterns’ designers were generally unnamed, the names and trademarks of manufacturers featured prominently on their front covers, along with the yarns they promoted. Drawings and, later, photographs of the knitted items these yarns would make sought to capture knitters’ attention. Cheap to buy, available wherever yarns were sold, pattern leaflets brought the latest knitwear fashions within reach of anyone who could afford the materials and time to make them. Mass-produced, ephemeral, and multimodal, their meanings communicated collectively by words, images, colour, and spatial layout (), they inhabit the same print ecology () as popular women’s magazines. Along with women’s magazines, they provide insights into the interests and values of the ordinary women they targeted, contributing to understandings of daily life in twentieth-century Britain – in relation to fashion and textile history in particular [Fig. 1].

Like women’s magazines, pattern leaflets are serialised: they are published in runs or series, over an extended period of time. Like magazines, therefore, they enable researchers to map change and continuity over a given timespan – the KLP set out to test whether the crowdsourced data could be used in this way. Yet there is one important distinction between leaflets’ seriality and the seriality of magazines. Leaflets, although they are numbered in order of publication, are not dated. In this respect, the seriality that defines each as a periodical operates differently, for whereas magazines appear on specified, predetermined days, evenly spaced by weeks or months, pattern leaflets have a more nebulous temporality: each follows the last in numerical order, yet their connection to calendar time is neither fixed nor explicit. Instead, their seriality manifests in their continually evolving form, which paradoxically [repeats] itself while at the same time becoming something new . Within each issue of each series of leaflets, the name of the producer and their trademark remain constant, along with the constitutive sections of the patterns themselves.
Materials list, tension and measurements, abbreviations, instructions, and image/s showing the finished item or items.
Undergoing continuous renewal are the designs and the yarns they promote, which, marking advances in fashion and technological production, measure a more abstract sense of temporality than is apparent through [the leaflets’] material form . To leaflets’ consumers, the absence of issue dates represents a compromise, between the ephemerality of fashion and the practical necessity for a knitted garment or other item – the making of which involves (often costly) materials, effort, skill, and time – to last. Although knitwear fashions, like serialised print, are designed to pass from the present into the past , undated pattern leaflets imbue the knitwear they promote with an implicit timelessness that promises to justify the expenditure and efforts of the knitter. To researchers of knitting leaflets however, the absence of issue dates introduces a complication – to map trends in their evolution over time, we must establish when they were published. This, as we shall see, could not be done using the methods trialled.

The particular challenge that the KLP set out to address is a direct consequence of pattern leaflets’ seriality. Along with other periodicals, they constitute a vastly underexplored (), unmanageable plenitude of texts () too numerous for one individual to read in their entirety. Previously, periodicals scholars addressed this challenge by sampling.
For instance, Cynthia White drew up a list of all women’s magazines published between 1800 and 1962, selected 42 titles for detailed analysis, and sampled these at intervals of 25 years in the nineteenth century, 10 years between 1900 and the Second World War, and 5 years during the post-war period, ‘the intervals being progressively compressed to allow for the accelerating pace of social change’ . Janice Winship used ‘personal and social’ criteria to select three titles for close analysis (Woman’s Own had the highest circulation of a weekly, Cosmopolitan had the highest circulation of a monthly, Spare Rib had a greater influence than its circulation figures would indicate, and she happened to be reading all three at the time) .
Following the advent of searchable, digitised archives around the turn of the twenty-first century however, some have pioneered computational methods of reading. Special issues of the Journal of European Periodical Studies, See .
The Journal of Modern Periodical Studies, See .
and Media History,
See .
issued during the 2010s, testify to the growing interest in these methods. Along with articles in Digital Humanities journals, including Digital Humanities Quarterly, See , , and .
these publications represent an expanding intersection between periodical studies and the Digital Humanities. A number of these studies use optical character recognition (OCR)-supported keyword searches to produce “distant readings” that map trends in the contents and appearance of large corpuses over time .
These, in turn, can draw attention to trends within wider culture . Caution is urged, by scholars who emphasise that distant readings can blur details and generalise , and that engaging with print forms digitally can result in us losing sight of their structure, layout, and materiality, and how these change over time . As Eleanor Reed demonstrates, the quality of the paper on which a magazine is printed reveals much about its status within the market and the wider conditions of its production . Nevertheless, to the extent that digitally produced distant readings can plot the larger structures underpinning a corpus , thereby providing context for close analysis or even helping to select texts to be read in close detail, they have methodological value . The KLP set out to establish whether twentieth-century trends in knitwear design and the contents and appearance of knitting pattern leaflets could be mapped through the quantitative analysis of data crowdsourced on Zooniverse.

Yet while the development of OCR technology has enabled the use of keywords to search and analyse large bodies of digitized written text (e.g. ), image content, which cannot yet be ‘read’ in the same way, remains less well scrutinized . This creates an additional challenge for scholars of heavily illustrated periodicals – the genre to which pattern leaflets belong – since distant readings drawn solely from their written text are necessarily limited. Approaches to addressing this challenge have included the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify and distinguish between images, Laure Thompson and David Mimno found that a CNN could identify visual characteristics of Dada images and distinguish between the pages of Dada journals and non-Dada journals ‘with a degree of accuracy that exceeds random chance’ . See also .
and Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (CLIP) to identify and analyse images that lack (manually added) metadata . These methods are in their infancy however and their accuracy is limited . For instance – although CNNs can distinguish photographs from illustrations, cluster visually similar advertisements, and […] identify buildings, cartoons, chess problems, crowds, faces, logos, maps, and weather reports on historical images taken from digitized newspapers , they cannot yet ‘read’ images in the detail of which humans are capable.
The KLP piloted online crowdsourcing, therefore, on the basis that the labour involved was that in which human-based analysis exceeds that of machine intelligence . In this respect, the project drew on GLAM initiatives such as Libraries and Archives Canada Co-Lab, a tool allowing anyone with an internet connection to explore Library and Archives Canada’s digitized collections and then tag, describe, translate, or transcribe them and What’s the Score at the Bodleian? (2012–2016): a project in which online volunteers inputted data from over 4000 uncatalogued, digitized musical scores . As we shall see, the KLP’s success in engaging an enthusiastic and knowledgeable community with a digitised collection of historical sources has considerable relevance for the GLAM sector.

The KLP was run on Zooniverse, a free, open source, online citizen science platform used to crowdsource data from and about large quantities of digitised content. Although established and used primarily by researchers within the sciences and social sciences, the platform also hosts humanities projects, which allow researchers within this field to generate data repositories that can be searched for quantitative answers to historical questions . To build a project, researchers upload subjects – files containing digitized content – onto Zooniverse and develop workflows of classification tasks – questions or transcription exercises – that are completed by members of the platform’s 1.7 million-strong registered volunteer community . Classifications are stored in a database, for downloading once the project is complete. One obvious potential issue with crowdsourcing as a data-collection method is quality assurance: ensuring that the classifications are accurate. For this reason, each task is performed on each subject multiple times, by different volunteers working independently of each other (): aggregated, their responses allow researchers to accept the majority consensus, identify points of disagreement, or simply see what the crowd thinks. Besides performing tasks, volunteers can engage with each other and researchers, by leaving comments on the project’s Talk boards and as ‘notes’ on individual subjects. The KLP showed that besides providing a nexus of community (Van Hyning et al, 2017, §1.2) these boards are a source of valuable feedback on the design of a project and can reveal limitations in its methods.

div.head: The dataset
div.p: The dataset surveyed in the KLP comprised images from 3208 scanned knitting pattern leaflets belonging to the KCG. Only the front covers and pages showing completed items were included – pages containing instructions for making the items were not. This is because the patterns are available only to KCG members, on whose subscriptions the charity relies, and cannot be shared on a public platform. Paper copies of these leaflets belong to the KCG’s archive of well over 50,000 knitting and crochet-related publications (), which is housed with the rest of its Collection in Yorkshire. These publications come from three principal sources. In 2014, UK-based yarn and thread manufacturer Coats PLC donated their pattern archive – about 10,000 leaflets by Coats and Patons or Patons & Baldwin, which merged with Coats in 1960 . Others are personal donations () or were bought in charity shops by the volunteers who maintain the Collection. Composed thus, the KCG’s archive of leaflets, and consequently the dataset, is neither balanced nor representative of the market as a whole, in terms of brand and era. The impossibility of collecting a sample of every knitting pattern leaflet ever printed in the UK precludes correcting this. It does, however, represent the output of three significant yarn and pattern manufacturers, along with what knitters and their families thought worth keeping, and what, simply, survived.

The scans in the dataset were produced by the KCG Publications Curator Barbara Smith, as part of an ongoing project to make the Collection more accessible. In total, there are ~54,000 pattern leaflets in the Collection; ~18,000 are out of copyright, or the KCG have permission to scan. By the autumn of 2022, when the KLP was built, ~3,700 complete patterns had been scanned, along with the front covers of an additional ~5,000 – these feature in catalogues on the KCG’s website, for members to download and browse. The order in which complete patterns are scanned is determined by the order in which they are requested. Most are patterns for women; patterns for babies, children, and men feature in the catalogues, but because these are rarely requested, fewer have been scanned in full . These factors further unbalance the KLP dataset: it contains only patterns that can legally be scanned and have been requested by KCG members and is biased towards women’s knitwear. Furthermore, 45 scans were removed before the dataset was uploaded. Pattern leaflets, like any cultural product, can contain material reflective of wider prejudice. I chose not to include these in the KLP, as they could upset participants or be downloaded and shared in other contexts.

div.head: Methods
div.p: To determine whether Zooniverse could be used to crowdsource quantifiable data about the contents and appearance of knitting pattern leaflets, and whether this data could produce distant readings mapping their development over the twentieth century, the KLP captured information in three separate categories. These were: decade of publication, technical information relating to the patterns themselves, and non-technical information about the leaflets’ appearance. Since the first two categories would require distinct forms of expertise, I organised the project into three separate workflows – each tested whether the information it sought to collect could be crowdsourced.

Workflow 1 was a single task: a multiple-choice question asking volunteers to select the decade in which they thought a pattern leaflet had been published from a drop-down list. Included because pattern leaflets are undated, and publication dates are necessary for developments over time to be mapped, this workflow targeted volunteers with expertise in twentieth century knitting and fashion history.

Workflow 2 comprised questions about the type, design, and construction of the knitted items in the leaflets: this data would enable the evolution of these items to be mapped over time. Based on the pattern tagging system developed by Barbara Smith for cataloguing publications in the KCG Collection, this workflow targeted volunteers with technical knitting expertise. Leaflets containing multiple patterns could not easily be classified within this workflow, which was developed to collect data from one knitted item at a time, so these were identified by the first question and then retired. Subsequent questions formed a ‘tree’ identifying the item’s type, Garment, accessory, toy, trimming, item for a pet, item of homeware (if a garment) the age and gender of its intended wearer and features pertaining to its overall shape, E.g. sleeve length, neck shape design attributes, E.g. colourwork, cables and embellishments. E.g. pompoms, sequins, a fringe

Workflow 3 comprised mostly multiple-choice questions capturing non-technical information about each leaflet. After entering the name of the leaflet’s publisher and its series number into text boxes, volunteers selected whether or not it contained an image; whether the image was a drawing, photograph, or both; whether or not it contained colour; whether or not there was an item of technology in the image; whether or not there was a person in the image; whether or not the image was set out-of-doors. This data would show how the appearance of pattern leaflets developed over time [Figs. 2, 3, 4].

figure.head: A screenshot showing Workflow 1 – to complete the task, volunteers selected the decade of publication from the list on the right of the screen and then clicked ‘Done’ (green button) to submit or ‘Done & Talk’ (blue button) to submit and post a comment. Image reproduced by kind permission of the Knitting & Crochet Guild.

A screenshot showing Workflow 2 – to complete this task, volunteers selected the attributes of the garment (a vest for a teenage girl) from the drop-down list on the right. Image reproduced by kind permission of the Knitting & Crochet Guild.

A screenshot showing Workflow 3 – to complete this task, volunteers selected ‘Yes’ or ‘No’ in response to the question ‘Is there an image on this leaflet?’ and then clicked ‘Next’ to move onto the following task. Image reproduced by kind permission of the Knitting & Crochet Guild.

div.p: Two aims motivated this division of the workflows. Firstly, I hoped that, if volunteers could choose to answer questions that matched their own expertise, the risk of mistakes and disagreements would be lessened. Secondly, the ‘non-expert’ workflow aimed to foster inclusivity by enabling those without specialist expertise to participate. Additional help and guidance for each task were available in a Field Guide containing further explanations and examples.

To reach a consensus on each classification, each subject passed through each workflow five times. Where three or more separate classifications were the same, consensus was reached. Volunteers were invited to engage with each other and myself on the project’s Talk boards – including a ‘Memories’ Talk board, included to encourage older participants to share memories of the leaflets or of knitting more generally. This aspect of the project drew on popular crowdsourcing initiatives such as StoryCorps, the Listening Project, and Life in a Day . The project was launched on 26 September 2023 and concluded on 6 October 2023, when all subjects had been classified. Ethics approval was gained from Brunel University’s CBASS Research Ethics Committee on 20 May 2022. The data were downloaded and analysed in Microsoft Excel.

div.head: Results and Discussion
div.p: A pilot, the KLP explored three questions. Is it possible to crowdsource data from knitting pattern leaflets on Zooniverse? Can crowdsourced data, analysed quantitatively, reveal trends in knitting pattern leaflets over time? What lessons does this project offer to future research? The following responds to these questions in turn.

div.head: Is it possible to crowdsource data from knitting pattern leaflets on Zooniverse?
div.p: In short – it’s complicated. As I have noted, the quantitative data crowdsourced by the KLP were flawed and, while these flaws usefully highlight ways in which the methods it piloted could be improved, unfortunately they suggest that it may not be possible to crowdsource the kinds of data I set out to collect on Zooniverse. I discuss this below. More optimistically, the KLP suggested that Zooniverse could successfully be used to engage knowledgeable and enthusiastic audiences with knitting pattern leaflets (and by extension other historic print forms) and to crowdsource valuable qualitative data about them: in particular, memories that enrich understandings of how they were used and the cultures in which they circulated.

Evidence of the KLP’s success in audience engagement lies, firstly, in the speed with which the volunteers completed the tasks. 575 participated and the project was completed in just 11 days – a remarkably short amount of time, according to a member of the team who manage Zooniverse (we thought it would be popular, but it all happening within a week [sic] is amazing! ). Further to this, comments on subject notes offer insights into volunteers’ skills and expertise, along with why they enjoyed taking part. “I classed this as lace and I think it’s a knitted grid, not crochet, because I think it looks flatter than crochet […] it looks like the dark stripes were embroidered not worked with a crochet hook” wrote one volunteer about a woman’s short-sleeved jumper,
Participant 1, “Subject 89803457” comment, 29 September 2023. demonstrating strong expertise in relation to fabric construction. “Knit in pieces using Fair Isle method, front and back would have been the same in construction” wrote another,
Participant 2, “Subject 89806351” comment, 29 September 2023.
revealing their own experience of knitting pullovers. Both comments, which carefully explain the rationale behind the classifications in question, speak to thoughtful, detailed engagement by expert and experienced knitters. Further enjoyment seems to have been gained from community building through peer-to-peer knowledge exchange. I am curious about if the [price of a leaflet] represents an accurate overview of knitwear costs in that era or is a one-off. I look forward to learning from anyone who sees something else wrote one volunteer, inviting others to share their own findings – two did.
Participant 4, “I Took A Guess on the Decade – What Do You Think?” Talk board, 28 September 2023.
Again, this exchange reveals close engagement and interest, articulated through curiosity and a desire to learn. A final marker of engagement, the tasks prompted critical reflection. That’s cheeky! You have to buy another pattern for the jumper if you want this cardigan to be a twinset commented one volunteer, in response to a sales-boosting technique.
Participant 3, “Subject 89801338” comments, 1 October 2023.
While working on this project I have been struck by how these vintage patterns seemed only to cater for the very slim. […] It’s good to see a design for someone who is a little larger.
Participant 5, “Sizing” Talk board, 2 October 2023.
It is clear that the KLP succeeded in engaging a community of skilled and experienced knitters, who enjoyed the tasks, cared and about getting them right, and developed their own knowledge and reading practices through taking part.

I have stated that volunteers were encouraged to share memories of pattern leaflets and knitting on a dedicated ‘Memories’ Talk board. 10 did, and others posted their recollections on subject notes. Among these were memories of adapting patterns in imported UK magazines so that they could be knitted with the wools available in Australia,
Participant 1, “Memories” Talk board, 29 September 2023
a father using machine knitting to supplement his income from the British Broadcasting Corporation,
Participant 6, “Memories” Talk board, 28 September 2023
and a mother and grandmother designing patterns for women’s magazines.
Participant 7, “Memories” Talk board, 26 September 2023
Patterns for children’s cardigans, with buttons on the left if made for a girl and on the right if made for a boy, prompted two volunteers to share their remembered frustration at what one described as a “silly” clothing convention.

p.quote: Who decided girls and boys need the buttons the other way round. I got fed up of trying to work out which it was and just made them all the same. Participant 3, “Who is the garment for?” Talk board, 2 October 2023.

When I was young childrens raincoats had 2 sets of buttons and buttonholes so they could go either way, and be handed down families. Isn’t it all silly? Participant 8, “Who is the garment for?” Talk board, 2 October 2023.
I’d forgotten about the raincoats. Participant 3, “Who is the garment for?” Talk board, 2 October 2023.

div.p:
This sharing of memories was a source of enjoyment for some volunteers. I still have some of my mother’s patterns from the 40s and 50s and my own from the 60s and 70s wrote one, A very enjoyable walk down memory lane.
Participant 9, “Mother’s patterns” Talk board, 27 September 2023.
I have enjoyed taking part in this project so much wrote another.

p.quote:
Now in my seventies, I was taught to knit by my Mum when I was about six years old and have a vivid memory of sitting in my Gran’s lap, chanting ‘In, round, through, off!’ […] We had no television, so I spent most of my time knitting […] I sold gloves to my family and relations and still have the pattern which I used. I was delighted to see the pattern in one of the tasks .
Participant 21, private message on Zooniverse to Eleanor Reed, 4 October 2023.

div.p: Exchanges and comments like these are immensely valuable. By providing insights into consumers’ reception of the pattern leaflets, they work to flesh out the communities and cultures within which they circulated, enriching understandings of the KCG’s Collection and bringing it to life. Although these memories, along with volunteers’ technical and critical insights into the leaflets and their history, were not the principal data the KLP sought to collect, they turned out to be among the most useful and usable. Their implications for future research are discussed in the Conclusion.

div.head: Can crowdsourced data, analysed quantitatively, reveal trends in knitting pattern leaflets (and similar print forms) over time?
div.p: Disappointingly, the KLP could not determine whether data crowdsourced on Zooniverse, analysed quantitatively, could reveal trends in the dataset and others like it, as the data were flawed. The data collected via workflow 1 were extracted in full. The data collected via workflows 2 and 3 were enormous, so the following datapoints were extracted: from workflow 2, data pertaining to five design attributes (bobbles, cables, lace, ribbing, and stranded colour) and from workflow 3, data pertaining to visual layout. As the tables in the Appendix show, in each workflow a lack of consensus (at least 3/5 agreement) was reached on too great a proportion of the classifications for the data to be useable. Checks of the dataset and analysis of comments left on Talk boards and subject notes attribute volunteers’ lack of consensus to three issues. In workflow 1, the level of expertise required to complete the classification task was too specialised. In workflow 2, the information needed to complete the classifications was not visible on some of the subjects. In workflow 3, the wording of the questions was insufficiently clear.

div.head: Workflow 1: decade identification – even experts struggled
div.p:
To determine the decade in which each pattern leaflet had been published, volunteers were asked to select a decade from the 1900s to the 1980s from a drop-down list. To help them, the Field Guide suggested visual context Including models’ hairstyles and make-up. and currency
Leaflets priced in pounds, shillings, and pence will have been published before the switch to decimal in 1971.
as indicators of the publication decade, highlighted some characteristic design features of knitwear by decade, and pointed out that leaflets promoting patterns for the armed forces are likely to have been from the 1910s (First World War) or the 1940s (Second World War). Since it would, however, be impossible to provide all of the information needed to identify the decade in which a pattern leaflet was published, this task was promoted within communities whose members were thought likely to be knowledgeable about twentieth-century knitwear fashions,
The Knitting & Crochet Guild, Knitting History Forum, Historic Knitting (on Facebook), Fleece to Fashion (Glasgow University).
the idea being to increase the probability that volunteers with appropriate expertise would participate.
It was not possible to determine how many of the volunteers who undertook this workflow had been recruited from these communities.
Unfortunately, as Table 1 in the Appendix shows, no consensus was reached on 20% of the dataset. To determine why, I checked two random samples – 16 in the ‘consensus’ group (two from each decade) and 16 in the ‘no consensus’ group. These checks suggested that the task of dating the leaflets was too difficult, even for expert volunteers, for the following reasons.

Firstly, completed items are sometimes pictured without any visual context. Five of the 16 leaflets in the ‘no consensus’ sample belong to this category. Priced in pre-decimal currency, they were published before 1971. Nevertheless, determining their decade of publication is challenging, because the illustrations showing the items made using the patterns they contain (two cardigans, three pairs of bed socks, four tablemats, and four scarves) lack the context that, as the Field Guide explained, would help. With the exception of the bed socks, which are pictured on feet emerging from beneath nightgowns or bedsheets, each of the garments is unmodelled, and all are pictured against a plain backdrop. Lacking clues such as model’s other clothing and hairstyle, or interior furnishings, they do not obviously belong to any decade [Fig. 6].

figure.head: A leaflet containing patterns for bed socks. Photographed without visual context, the socks are difficult to date. Image reproduced by kind permission of the Knitting & Crochet Guild.

div.p:
Secondly, volunteers are less likely to have had prior contact with leaflets from earlier decades. Within the ‘consensus’ sample, those which were agreed to have been published during the 1910s and 1920s are not, in fact, from those decades. Those classified as being from the 1910s are from the 1920s,
One is for a woman’s cardigan with a matching hat, pictured on a woman with a short, bobbed hairstyle distinctive of that decade. The other is for a crocheted jumper with a tie around its waist, a design popular during the decade’s early years.
and those classified as being from the 1920s are from the 1930s.
A woman’s suit (long skirt with matching jacket) and a woman’s bed or dressing jacket.
Of the remaining 12 in the sample, all of which are from the 1940s onwards, 11 were correctly dated and one was possibly correct.
A leaflet containing a pattern for a crocheted bedspread. This was agreed to have been from the 1970s, perhaps because the sample in the illustration was made in yarn that is avocado green, a colour associated with that era due to its distinctive bathroom designs. The leaflet is priced at 6d however, which means that it would have need to have been printed during 1970 (decimalisation came into effect on 15 February 1971).
The suggestion that volunteers may have struggled to date earlier leaflets because they had not encountered them before is inferred by the Talk board comments and subject notes sharing memories, discussed above. By no means all who shared memories gave their ages, but a small number did and a few recalled childhoods in the 1950s. The parents of people who are now in their seventies or eighties would themselves have been children during the 1920s and 1930s and therefore less likely to have saved patterns from these decades. The qualitative data suggesting that volunteers drew their knowledge of historic knitwear from patterns in their mothers’ collections indicates that they may have had less exposure to those from earlier decades and would therefore have found these harder to date.

div.head: Workflow 2: design features – required information not visible
div.p: Workflow 2 sought to collect data that, in combination with data on publication decade from workflow 1, could be used to map trends in knitwear fashions, by identifying shifts in the popularity of certain knitwear design features. These included length and style of sleeve, shape of neckline, the presence or otherwise of fastenings (e.g. buttons, zips) and embellishments (e.g. sequins, ribbons, pompoms), and patterns in the texture and colour of the knitted fabric itself, such as cables, ribbing, colourwork, and intarsia. To extract this data, volunteers answered questions including “What neck shape does this garment have?” and “What embellishments does this item have?” and then selected their answers from a drop-down box. Again, no consensus was reached on too many of the classifications for the data to be useable (see Table 2, Appendix).

Comments on subject notes indicate that no consensus was reached on classifications pertaining to knitwear design features because images of finished items were either incomplete or lacked sufficient detail.

list.item: The neckline is not visible. Participant 10, “Subject 89803243” comment, 3 October 2023.
Could be a zip fastening, but not visible. Participant 11, “Subject 89806297” comment, 2 October 2023.
Swimsuit with no view of the front. Participant 12, “Subject 89803344” comment, 1 October 2023.

I can’t quite tell whether the dark dashed line at the top neck is actually cord threaded through the ribbing […] or it it’s done with stranding. Participant 13, “Subject 89801327” comment, 26 September 2023.

I’m not sure what the trim is. I think there was a wavy cord trim that might have been called something like ric-rac. It might be that, or it could be embroidered. Participant 3, “Subject 89820529” comment, 2 October 2023.
Difficult to see the cuffs and other stitches as the wool creates the striped pattern. I have classed this item as striped for this reason. Participant 14, “Subject 89803248” comment, 3 October 2023.
It is unclear if the back wave effect is applique or a textured stitch. Participant 14, “Subject 89820245” comment, 3 October 2023.

div.p: Checks support what these comments indicate, which is that these features were too difficult to classify from illustrations alone. The first refers to a cardigan, modelled by a woman wearing a scarf that completely covers its neckline [see Fig. 7]. The second also refers to a cardigan, which could well be fastened by a zip – but this is impossible to confirm because the fastening is concealed by its fluffy texture. The third refers to a swimsuit, modelled by a boy with his back to the camera. The “dark dashed line” around the neckline of the fourth, a woman’s jumper, blurs when you zoom in. Because the trim on the fifth, a woman’s cardigan, is the same colour as the rest of the fabric, it blends in too well to be identified as ric-rac or embroidery. The sixth, a woman’s jumper, has been knitted in variegated (colour-changing) yarn – the random stripes this produces make it difficult to distinguish stitch patterns. Finally, the quality of the photograph makes it hard to establish whether the waves referred to on the seventh, a woman’s jumper, were knitted into the fabric or sewn on (appliquéd). The observations made in these comments along with their technical language suggest that they were made by volunteers with expertise in knitwear design, who might reasonably be expected capable of collecting data of this kind. Their efforts were hampered by the leaflets themselves – owing to the position of the model or their other clothing, the attributes of the fabric, or simply the quality of the image, they were prevented from classifying them.

figure.head: A leaflet containing a pattern for a woman’s cardigan. The model’s scarf completely covers the neckline, making the latter’s shape impossible to determine. Image reproduced by kind permission of the Knitting & Crochet Guild.

div.head: Workflow 3: basic visual data – task expectations and terminology were unclear
div.p: Aimed at non-experts, workflow 3 sought to collect data relating to the visual composition of knitting pattern leaflets that, in combination with the data on publication decade, would support a quantitative analysis of how these periodicals changed in appearance over time. Like the front covers of women’s magazines, the front covers of knitting pattern leaflets work to grab the attention of potential consumers. Most are dominated by an image showcasing the item or items made by following the instructions inside. Like magazine covers, these images work the pattern or patterns into wider networks of cultural codes. For instance, an expensive-looking car might associate a knitted item with material luxury; an out-of-doors setting might associate it with an active lifestyle; an indoor setting invokes comfort in the home or workplace. The presence of a model works to create a personal connection between the knitting leaflet and the consumer. Finally, the medium of the image itself speaks to developments in image reproduction: we might reasonably expect the number of photographs to rise and the number of drawings to fall over the period, the number of leaflets printed in colour to increase, and the number of images taken out-of-doors to rise, thanks to improvements in photographic technology. To see if it would be possible to crowdsource data that would allow these visual trends to be mapped, volunteers were asked the following six multiple-choice questions.

list.item: Is there an image on this leaflet? (Yes / No)
Is the image a drawing, a photograph, or both? (Drawing / Photograph / Both)
Does the leaflet contain colour? (Yes / No)
Is there an item of technology in the image? (Yes / No)
Is there a person in the image? (Yes / No)
Is the image set out-of-doors? (Yes / No)

div.p: Again, no consensus was reached on too great a proportion of the data for it to be useable (see Table 3, Appendix).

Comments on subject notes attribute the lack of consensus to volunteers’ confusion over how to answer the questions. Question 1 is the exception – I checked a random sample of five in the ‘no consensus’ group – all had images, and no comments highlighting difficulties were left. In relation to question 2, there seems to have been confusion over what counted as a drawing:

p.quote: In response to the question “Drawing” or “Photograph”, I’m choosing “Both” because, as well as containing a photograph of a young boy modelling the knitted item, the leaflet also includes a P&B Wools beehive logo which evidently isn’t a photograph. Participant 15, “Subject 89810186” comment, 27 September 2023

I have a few basic questions about what is considered a "Drawing" on the leaflets. Is a logo like a Beehive or a Robin considered a Drawing? Is graphic text printed over top of a photograph considered a Drawing? Participant 22, “Feedback” Talk board, 27 September 2023

div.p:
When I wrote that question, the drawings I had in mind were the illustrations showing completed items on older leaflets. These comments highlighted that publishers’ logos and even the KCG’s watermark, which is added to scans to prevent unauthorised sharing, could be interpreted as drawings as well. The presence or absence of colour, recorded by question 3, also seems to have been open to interpretation. “If a pattern is in black and white but there is writing or a stamp on it that has colour do we still say yes?” Participant 23, “Help!” Talk board, 27 September 2023
asked one volunteer, referring to content added to leaflets by retailers or knitters. Likewise, whether or not the image contained a person, recorded by question 5, was open to conjecture. “I answered ‘no’ to a person in the photo as there is no face” Participant 16, “Subject 89800729” comments, 27 September 2023
wrote one volunteer, about an image of legs modelling knee socks. “There are human hands shown here, so I selected ‘Yes’, that there was a person in this photo” Participant 17, “Subject 89820146” comments, 27 September 2023 wrote another, taking the opposite approach to classifying an image on a leaflet containing glove patterns. Non-human models including dolls and dogs prompted further uncertainty. “I wasn't sure if dolls count as ‘persons’!” (Participant 18, “Subject 89820221” comments, 27 September 2023); “There is no ‘person’ in the image but the wearers are included in the photograph (the dogs)” (Participant 19, “Subject 89805298” comments, 26 September 2023) For question 6, there was confusion over whether or not ‘outdoor settings’ should include those recreated in photographic studios.

p.quote: Image is obviously photographed in a studio meant to look as if it is taken out-of-doors, so is this ‘set’ out-of-doors? Participant 20, “Subject 89806285” comment, 27 September 2023

In response to the question of whether the photograph is indoors or outside, unless the setting is obviously outside (i.e. on location), I’m selecting indoors (i.e. in a photographic studio) even if the “set” is trying to simulate an outdoor location. Participant 15, “Subject 89804824” comment, 27 September 2023

div.p: Question 4, however, seems to have caused the most confusion. This surfaced, firstly, in questions and comments in relation to whether certain items ‘counted’ as technology.

p.quote: Do toys count as pieces of technology or no? Participant 24, “Subject 89803544” comment, 26 September 2023
Are buttons considered technology? Participant 25, “Help!” Talk board, 26 September 2023
Is a golf club ‘technology’? Participant 26, “Subject 89809293” comment, 26 September 2023
Can the bicycle be considered an item of technology? Participant 27, “Help” Talk board, 27 September 2023

div.p: Other volunteers shared their own definitions or technology, or sought reassurance that these were correct:

p.quote: I have assumed toys or children’s games do not constitute ‘items of technology’ for these purposes. Participant 28, “Subject 89805362” comment, 26 September 2023

Are watches considered technology? I answered "no" to the image containing technology, but is this wrong? Also, one of the images I worked on today had a bow (for shooting arrows with) in the picture — would that be considered technology? I guess I'm thinking of technology being something from the 1950's onward. . .? Participant 29, “Subject 89802831” comment, 27 September 2023

div.p: One volunteer declared that, since clothing itself is produced using technology, they were classifying every image as containing technology:

p.quote: I'd go as far as calling a needle and thread technology. Because it is spun out of the human imagination and created by manipulation of their environment. So this is going to be a blanket yes in that category from me, since everything I've seen so far includes some type of garment. Participant 25, “Help!” Talk board, 28 September 2023

div.p: The comments discussed here outline two key issues relating to project design. Firstly, lack of clarity about how I expected the leaflets’ visual design to be interpreted. Although there are no comments to back this up, it seems possible that volunteers struggled with question 1 because I did not specify what was meant by ‘image’. Volunteers struggled with questions 2 and 3 because I did not establish exactly which visual content counted as part of the image. They found question 5 difficult because I did not explain whether ‘person’ included isolated body parts and whether non-human models counted too. Likewise, question 6 presented difficulties because I failed to account for the practice, extremely common in pre-1960s patterns, of photographing knitwear in ‘outdoor’ locations created on indoor sets. Question 4 raised a separate issue with project design, however. The decision not to define ‘technology’ was deliberate, as I did not want to tie participants to my own understanding of what is, after all, a very broad term. I therefore limited the parameters to the following guidance in the help text: “Items of technology might include: a vehicle, a telephone, a lighting fixture such as a desk lamp, a domestic appliance such as a vacuum cleaner.” Participants’ confusion, which contributed to the lack of consensus, shows that this was a mistake.

div.head: What lessons does the KLP offer to future research?
div.p: Noting the importance of piloting new methods and that even flawed data can be useful, Suphan Kirmizialtin and David Joseph Wrisley state that tools are often not a perfect fit for the historical source material we possess and the results we obtain teach us a significant amount about our objects of study . While the KLP demonstrated that Zooniverse may not be an effective platform for crowdsourcing quantitative data from knitting pattern leaflets, it suggested that the platform could nevertheless be used to collect other forms of data from them. Its lessons for future research are as follows.

Firstly, and with relevance for GLAM organisations as well as academics, the KLP highlighted the effectiveness of Zooniverse for crowdsourcing qualitative data. The strength of volunteers’ enthusiasm for the tasks along with the care and thoughtfulness with which they completed them indicate that future projects of this kind would recruit well, and that engagement would be strong. As I have noted, the memories volunteers shared have immense value, as ‘hidden’ knowledge that could transform understandings of pattern leaflets’ use and circulation during the twentieth century. Furthermore, their comments demonstrated critical engagement with both the leaflets themselves and the cultures in which they circulated. A future Zooniverse project could, these outputs suggest, generate material to enrich an archive or exhibition of popular print forms from the twentieth century, by collecting new information about how they were used and understood by people who bought and read them, along with critical responses from a wider audience.

Secondly, some forms of data are too specialised to be crowdsourced, even by expert groups. The flaws in the data collected through workflow 1 indicate that the task of determining the publication decade of each pattern leaflet might more accurately have been undertaken by individuals who work closely and consistently with the dataset, and who have therefore gained a ‘feel’ for decade of publication. This could have been managed in two ways. Either the leaflets could have been dated before being uploaded to Zooniverse, or this workflow could have been completed on the platform, but before the project’s public launch. Expert classifiers might have done a ‘first pass’ – dating the leaflets about whose publication decade they felt confident and identifying those that are harder to date. They could then have reached conclusions about the latter group through discussion.

Thirdly, researchers should check during the development stage that the data they are crowdsourcing are available and accessible. Comments on workflow 2 showed that to collect data pertaining to the design and structure of knitwear, the volunteers needed access to the patterns themselves. The difficulties they experienced show that it was too ambitious of me to expect even experienced knitters to glean information about garment construction and stitch patterns from the cover illustrations of knitting leaflets alone. A future project using the same dataset would either need to make the patterns available as well, or limit data collection to information that is accessible even in an incomplete image, such as type of item.

The KLP’s final lesson is that crowdsourcing to be effective, instructions need to be clear and specific. Participants need to know exactly how they are expected to interpret the information they are presented with, and exactly what they are being asked to collect. Volunteers’ confusion over which visual content they were being asked to classify in workflow 3 could have been avoided had I thought more carefully about what, for instance, constituted an ‘image’ – the picture showing the item that could be made using the pattern, the publisher’s logo, or both. And it was a mistake to leave ‘technology’ open to interpretation. Based on my own knowledge of twentieth century knitting patterns, I could have asked, instead, whether the image contained (for instance) a vehicle, a telephone, a lighting fixture, a television, a radio, an item of sports equipment, or a weapon.

div.head: Conclusion – what might a more effective project look like?
div.p: I want to conclude this case study on a positive note, by using the above lessons to imagine what a more effective version of the KLP might look like. Firstly, workflow 1 would be undertaken by a select group of experts in twentieth century knitting history. Secondly, on the basis that the pattern instructions in the KCG dataset cannot be made publicly available, workflow 2 would capture just the category of each item (garment, accessory, homeware, toy, item of a pet). Although more limited, this data would still show trends in knitting over the twentieth century, within this dataset of leaflets at least. The tasks in workflow 3 would specify more precisely how volunteers were expected to interpret the leaflets’ visual contents. These changes would enable me to determine whether, in fact, quantitative data crowdsourced on Zooniverse can produce ‘big readings’ of the dataset. Such a project could, indeed, be run alongside a computational analysis of the leaflets, to gather visual data that would complement that collected through OCR-supported keyword searches of the written text. Finally, on the basis of the qualitative data collected by the KLP, I would promote the ‘Memories’ Talk board more and prompt volunteers explicitly to reflect critically on the pattern leaflets, to explore the potential of Zooniverse to collect these forms of data further.
